1/ GLM 5.3 at full 1M context on a single 8xH200 node. That didn't fit before.

Agentic serving is why it's hard: many concurrent requests, each with a long context that keeps growing. The GPU block pool is fixed, so the KV cache runs out of room. Something has to give. https://t.co/urdXTf5lv1

5/6 The payoff: under pressure, both requests keep decoding at partial residency instead of one waiting for a slot or re-prefilling itself. Higher concurrency across context lengths, and the full 1M context on hardware that couldn't hold it before.

Benchmarked on an OpenHands agentic workload. Landing in vLLM v0.30. Full writeup:
https://t.co/cc2MDLgC8V

6/6 Credit where it's due. @vllm_project's Hybrid HiSparse implementation was developed by @MatthewBonanni and Lucas Wilkinson at @RedHat, with Fares Obeid at @PrimeIntellect. Design input from Chao Lei at @AntGroup and @nick_lucche at @MistralAI. Performance work from Simon Veitner (Red Hat). Thanks to the HiSparse authors (https://t.co/mXMCCaUTyV) for the sparse offloading idea.

Takes a village.

Why offload KV cache to CPU at all? Because GPU memory is the one tier in the stack you can't expand, and often what's sitting in it is cold.

In a long-running session, vLLM eventually fills HBM and starts evicting KV blocks to make room. Drop the wrong ones and the model loses earlier context: it re-asks answered questions or contradicts itself, with no error, just quietly worse output.

But tool outputs and documents from many turns back don't need to stay resident every step. CPU offloading moves those cold blocks to host memory and pulls them back over DMA when a request needs them, freeing HBM for live work without dropping context.

It isn't free: a block fetched from CPU costs transfer latency versus one already on the GPU. But that's trading a little latency for capacity on the tier you can't grow, which is usually the right call.

A few links worth checking out in reply...

The overview, why the context wall happens and why offloading is the fix: https://t.co/8i2gf3pbAw

The how, enabling KV cache offloading in @vllm_project: https://t.co/c3xDXPkiY3

Sparse MLA only attends to the top-K tokens, so the rest of the KV need not live on the GPU. Hybrid HiSparse in vLLM builds on that, and a request keeps decoding after its KV stops fitting in HBM.

It keeps KV on the GPU while there is room. Under pressure a request releases its coldest pages to host memory, keeps a small hot buffer of what the indexer asks for, and keeps decoding instead of being preempted.

📊 Demonstrated on GLM 5.3, one 8× H200 node, full 1M context. Same host memory, configured concurrency 32: KV offloading kept 5-6 requests running. Hybrid HiSparse kept 19-25.

🔹 Hot pages are ordinary KV blocks from the same pool (Hybrid Memory Allocator)
🔹 One fused kernel resolves resident, hot and missing rows, CUDA-graph capturable
🔹 Prefix caching, OffloadingConnector, P/D imports and MTP keep working

Flow control is an admission layer for shared GPU inference.

Before a request gets routed to a model server, it's either admitted or held. Under saturation, priority decides which class of traffic advances, fairness spreads dispatch turns across tenants so no one gets starved, and ordering picks the next request. Lower-priority work waits instead of crowding out what matters.

Admission decides when a request runs. Routing decides where. Keeping those separate is the whole idea.

posts.text:
Almost everyone we talk to has picked a side here. Either you carve out dedicated pools and accept the idle GPUs, or you share capacity and hope nothing important gets stuck behind a batch job.

flow control in @_llm_d_ is trying to give you a third option. Admission control and priority policies, so the requests that actually matter still get served when things get tight.

Alexa's benchmarks are worth the click. Which way did your team go?

quotedTweet.text:
Dedicated GPU pools protect latency-sensitive products. The downside is that those GPUs are most likely underutilized. Shared GPU capacity is ideal, but the trade-off is losing your strict latency/SLO guarantees for high-priority requests.

That's why I'm excited about @_llm_d_ 's flow control feature. It manages request admission and multitenant priority policies for shared GPU capacity under pressure.

If you're interested in learning more, I ran some benchmarks here https://t.co/YDdMGsLEhb @RedHat_AI

Six weeks ago, serving DSpark in vLLM meant choosing a draft length for your traffic and living with it. Now you set that length once, and vLLM decides how much of the draft to verify every step. ✨

On DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, the first token of a 7-token draft survives verification more than 70% of the time. The last one, less than 10%.

📈 One config, adaptive verification on with num_speculative_tokens 7, holds the Pareto frontier from concurrency 1 to 256 on 8×B300. Long draft at low load, short at high load.

On main behind enable_adaptive_verification, for DSpark with a confidence head on Flash Attention or DSV4 attention. More backends and models are in bring-up. Thanks to Lucas Wilkinson (@RedHat_AI) and Ben Chislett (@NVIDIAAI), and to @deepseek_ai for DSpark and the varlen DeepGEMM indexer kernel.

How does a single-GPU RAG chatbot become a multi-workload inference platform?

Grace from Red Hat AI walks through the whole stack: AI Gateway, vLLM, and llm-d. Quantization, speculative decoding, cache-aware routing, and prefill/decode disaggregation, one step at a time.

In under 5 minutes:
